ModelCharacter: The defining Duffy: Spencer Lincoln's 35-foot built-down lobsterboat combined a fine forefoot, flat after sections and unusual speed with the sea-kindliness Maine fishermen demanded. It became one of the most successful fiberglass lobsterboat hulls ever and an enduring basis for high-quality Downeast cruisers.
DesignLineage: Spencer Lincoln designed the Duffy 35 in 1981.
Richard Duffy built a race-oriented example whose performance helped establish the model's reputation.
Atlantic Boat reports more than 370 Duffy 35 hulls built since 1982.
The Duffy 31 followed the 35's hull philosophy at smaller scale, while the later Duffy 37 was developed as a larger, faster evolution of the 35.
OwnershipCharacter: A proven commercial hull with excellent owner/builder knowledge and simple single-diesel propulsion, but individual cruiser finishes can be extremely sophisticated. Engine horsepower, speed, tankage and displacement should always be taken from the individual boat rather than assumed from the hull model.

It launched the Mainship line and became a widely recognized affordable cruising model.

ModelVariations.Description: The first 34 used the original salon, cockpit and bridge-extension arrangement and preceded the 34 II and 34 III.

ModelCharacter: The original 1978–82 Mainship 34 and the most traditional-looking of the three classic generations. It devotes the greatest length to the enclosed salon, has the shortest cockpit, and carries the long cabin-top/flybridge overhang far aft to shelter much of the cockpit.
DesignLineage: Introduced in 1978 as the Mainship 34 Diesel Cruiser/Motor Cruiser, commonly called the MK I.
Its defining layout is the longest salon and shortest aft cockpit of the classic 34 family, with a long flybridge/cabin-top overhang shading the cockpit.
The cockpit-oriented 34 II appeared in 1979 on the same basic hull but with substantially more cockpit and less salon.
Both early versions were superseded by the 34 III for 1983.
OwnershipCharacter: The simplest and most interior-focused classic 34. A single diesel and protected shaft keep propulsion straightforward; the long salon, extensive teak and long overhang make windows, deck/cabin-top moisture and exterior structure important survey areas.

ModelVariations.Name: Power versus motorsailer configuration
ModelVariations.Description: The Nomad is a pocket-trawler powerboat; the Kodiak is a pilothouse sailboat/motorsailer; the Wanderer was offered with or without a sailing rig. These are materially different use cases despite shared Nimble/Ted Brewer design language.

ModelCharacter: A highly unusual Ted Brewer-designed 32-foot pilothouse cruiser offered from the factory both with and without a sailing rig. In power-cruiser form it combines a single diesel, long encapsulated keel, 8'6" trailerable beam, shallow draft and bright trawler-like interior in a narrow, easily transported hull.
DesignLineage: The Wanderer was a later collaboration between Ted Brewer and Nimble builder Gerry Koch, appearing in the late 1990s.
Cruising World explicitly documented that the Wanderer was available with or without a mast.
The rigged version is properly understood as a motorsailer, while mastless examples are legitimate factory power cruisers rather than owner-converted sailboats.
The Wanderer is therefore retained inside B-Atlas, but its power-versus-motorsailer configuration must be verified on each individual listing.
OwnershipCharacter: Single-diesel simplicity, shallow draft and legal-width trailering are major strengths, but the narrow 8'6" beam limits interior and side-deck space. The very small production run means builder-specific components and documentation can be difficult, while standard Yanmar and marine systems remain supportable.

EvolutionNotes: Treat separately from later Nimbus Coupé models; aft-cabin accommodation and cockpit arrangement materially change buyer fit.
BScoutSignature: Compact Scandinavian all-weather cruiser combining a protected helm, multiple sleeping zones and efficient single-diesel ownership.
